results.content: We consider a federated class-incremental learning (FCIL) setting, where a central server aims to collaboratively train a global model with the assistance of K distributed clients. Each client k receives a sequence of classification tasks {D_k^(1), D_k^(2), ..., D_k^(t)}, where each task introduces a disjoint set of new classes. Upon the arrival of task t, the global model parameters θ_t are optimized to minimize the average loss over the union of all samples seen so far, i.e., 𝔻^t = ⋃_{s=1}^t ⋃_{k=1}^K D_k^(s), by solving min_θ (1/|𝔻^t|) Σ_{s=1}^t Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{i=1}^{N_k^(s)} L(f_k(x_{k,i}^(s); θ), y_{k,i}^(s)).
results.route_rationale: Modelling setup defining the FCIL training objective; a definition rather than a falsifiable assertion.

math_result.reasoning: The snippet defines an optimization objective for federated class-incremental learning. Checking internal consistency of the average-loss formulation: the global dataset is 𝔻^t = ⋃_{s=1}^t ⋃_{k=1}^K D_k^(s), and the objective is min_θ (1/|𝔻^t|) Σ_{s=1}^t Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{i=1}^{N_k^(s)} L(f_k(x_{k,i}^(s); θ), y_{k,i}^(s)). Since the tasks introduce disjoint sets of classes (stated in the text), the sample sets D_k^(s) are disjoint across tasks, so |𝔻^t| = Σ_{s=1}^t Σ_{k=1}^K N_k^(s), where N_k^(s) = |D_k^(s)| is the number of samples in client k's task-s dataset. The number of summands in the triple sum is exactly Σ_s Σ_k N_k^(s) = |𝔻^t|, so dividing by |𝔻^t| yields precisely the arithmetic mean loss over all samples seen so far — the normalization is consistent with the summation domain. No invalid algebra, no fractional-arithmetic error, no sign propagation issue, and no domain constraint violation (an average of losses is well-defined for any loss values). The subscript k on f_k is a minor notational ambiguity (the paper elsewhere optimizes global parameters θ_t shared across clients), but it is not a provably invalid mathematical operation and cannot be confirmed as an error from the snippet alone. This is a modelling definition, not a falsifiable derivation, and the definition is internally coherent.

results.content: In replay-based methods, each client maintains a memory buffer with a fixed budget of M samples. When task t arrives, the client selects up to N representative samples from each of the previous tasks {1, ..., t-1}, subject to the total memory constraint. The resulting memory set is denoted by B_k^(t-1) = ⋃_{s=1}^{t-1} {(x_{k,i}^(s), y_{k,i}^(s))}_{i=1}^N, where N is the number of samples stored per task and |B_k^(t-1)| ≤ M. The local training set on client k then becomes D_{k,train}^(t) = D_k^(t) ∪ B_k^(t-1), combining current and replayed samples. Based on these local datasets, the server updates the global model by minimizing the aggregated loss: min_θ Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{(x,y) ∈ D_{k,train}^(t)} L(f_k(x; θ), y).
results.route_rationale: Replay-buffer set definition with budget constraint; definitional, checked for internal consistency.

math_result.reasoning: This is a definitional/model-setup passage, and I find no derivation-invalidating mathematical error. (1) The memory-set definition B_k^(t-1) = ⋃_{s=1}^{t-1} {(x_{k,i}^{(s)}, y_{k,i}^{(s)})}_{i=1}^N is a well-defined union of N (or up to N) labeled samples per previous task s; assuming distinct data points across tasks, |B_k^(t-1)| = N·(t-1) (or fewer when the client selects fewer than N from a task), and the stated constraint |B_k^(t-1)| ≤ M is consistent with the fixed budget of M samples — the 'up to N per task' selection rule and the total-budget inequality are compatible (the budget caps the union; if N·(t-1) > M, the selection rule is implicitly truncated to respect |B| ≤ M). (2) The local training set D_{k,train}^{(t)} = D_k^(t) ∪ B_k^(t-1) is a standard, internally consistent union of current-task and replayed data. (3) The aggregated objective min_θ Σ_{k=1}^K Σ_{(x,y)∈D_{k,train}^{(t)}} L(f_k(x;θ), y) is a well-formed empirical-risk sum over clients' local datasets with a shared parameter θ; even if f_k varies per client, the sum is a valid objective in θ, and whether the server literally optimizes it (vs. clients doing local steps) is a procedural modeling simplification, not a mathematical error. Minor notational looseness ('up to N' vs. an i=1..N index, and the dependence of the buffer on the exact task arrival ordering) does not invalidate the definition. No invalid algebra, fractional manipulation, sign propagation, or domain-constraint violation is present; nothing here would require an erratum.

results.content: Inspired by Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we first generate a set of random orthogonal matrices: a client-specific matrix P_k^(i) ∈ ℝ^{|D_k^(i)| × |D_k^(i)|} for each client k and task i, and a globally shared matrix Q^(i) ∈ ℝ^{d × d}, where d denotes the dimension of the feature. Each client encrypts its local feature matrix X_k^(i) = M_g(D_k^(i)) via Inverse Singular Value Decomposition (ISVD):  X_k^(i)' = P_k^(i) X_k^(i) Q^(i), (1)
results.route_rationale: ISVD encryption transformation; dimension-consistency check on a definition.

math_result.reasoning: The equation X_k^(i)' = P_k^(i) X_k^(i) Q^(i) is dimensionally consistent and mathematically well-defined. P_k^(i) is |D_k|×|D_k|, X_k^(i) is |D_k|×d, and Q^(i) is d×d, so the product P_k X_k is |D_k|×d (valid matrix multiplication: (|D_k|×|D_k|)·(|D_k|×d)), and (P_k X_k) Q is (|D_k|×d)·(d×d) = |D_k|×d, matching the claimed shape of X_k^(i)'. Left-multiplication by the orthogonal matrix P_k applies a basis change along the sample (row) dimension, and right-multiplication by the orthogonal matrix Q^(i) applies a rotation in feature space (column dimension); both are well-defined linear transformations, and together they form a two-sided orthogonal transformation that preserves the Frobenius norm of X_k^(i). Since P_k and Q^(i) are stated to be orthogonal (invertible), the transformation is also invertible, consistent with the described encryption/decryption use case. The label 'Inverse Singular Value Decomposition (ISVD)' is a terminology choice rather than a mathematical claim embodied in the equation itself, and this is a definition/transformation step rather than a falsifiable theorem, so no derivation-invalidating flaw exists here. The dimensions check out and no algebraic, sign, or domain violation is present.

results.content: The server then aggregates all encrypted matrices into a global matrix X^(i)':  X^(i)' = concat{ X_k^(i)' | k = 1, ..., K }, (2)

math_result.reasoning: This equation is a definition (aggregation of per-client encrypted feature matrices via a concat operation), not a falsifiable theorem. Row-wise concatenation (vertical stacking) of K matrices, each of shape |D_k^(i)| × d, produces a matrix of shape (Σ_k |D_k^(i)|) × d, which is exactly the intended global matrix — the operation is dimensionally coherent because all client matrices share the same feature dimension d, and the row count accumulates additively. There is no algebraic manipulation, no fractions, no sign propagation, and no probability/domain constraint involved. The only mild caveat is that the direction of concatenation (row-wise vs column-wise) is not explicitly stated, but column-wise concat would require equal row counts, which does not hold here, so row-wise is the uniquely coherent reading and the definition is internally consistent. No derivation-invalidating error is present.

results.content: and performs SVD as follows:  X^(i)' = U^(i)' Σ^(i)' V^(i)'^⊤, (3)  where U^(i)' ∈ ℝ^{n × n}, Σ^(i)' ∈ ℝ^{n × d}, and V^(i)' ∈ ℝ^{d × d}, with n denoting the total number of samples from all clients.
results.route_rationale: Full SVD shape claim; standard result, dimension check.

math_result.reasoning: The snippet states X^(i)' = U^(i)' Σ^(i)' V^(i)'^T with U^(i)' in R^{n x n}, Sigma^(i)' in R^{n x d}, V^(i)' in R^{d x d}, for an n x d matrix X^(i)'. This is exactly the standard full (also called thin/complete) SVD of a real n x d matrix: U is n x n orthogonal, Sigma is n x d with nonnegative singular values on its diagonal (rectangular diagonal, zero off-diagonal entries), and V is d x d orthogonal. The product is well-defined: (n x n)(n x d) = n x d, then (n x d)(d x d) = n x d, matching the shape of X^(i)'. There is no dimension mismatch, no invalid algebra, and no domain violation. The decomposition exists for any real matrix with these dimensions, so this is a standard, correct result.

results.content: Next, the server extracts a submatrix of the left singular vectors for each client k by:  U_k^(i) = 𝕀_k(U^(i)') ∈ ℝ^{|D_k^(i)| × n}, (4)  where 𝕀_k(·) denotes a row selection function that returns the indices corresponding to client k's samples.

math_result.reasoning: The equation is a definition (a row-selection operator applied to a matrix), not a falsifiable theorem, and its stated dimensions are internally consistent. If U^(i)' ∈ R^(n×n), then selecting |D_k^(i)| rows yields exactly |D_k^(i)| rows and n columns, i.e., a matrix in R^(|D_k^(i)| × n) — matching the stated shape precisely. The row-selection function I_k(·) that returns the row indices corresponding to client k's samples is consistent with the standard SVD convention in which rows of the left singular vector matrix correspond to samples of the decomposed data matrix (n = total number of samples across clients); there is no indication of a transposed or mismatched convention. No algebraic manipulation, sign propagation, domain violation, or logical contradiction is present or provable from the snippet. Even if the SVD is only unique up to sign per column, that does not invalidate the shape or the selection definition.

results.content: To quantify the importance of local samples within the global latent space, client k computes a leverage score for the j-th sample of task i as:  τ_k^(i,j) = || e_{i,j}^⊤ U_k^(i) ||_2^2, (5)  where e_{i,j} denotes the j-th standard basis vector in task i. Notably, a higher leverage score indicates that the sample has a larger projection in the low-dimensional latent space, suggesting that it contributes more significantly to the global structure and is more representative.

math_result.reasoning: The definition τ_k^(i,j) = || e_{i,j}^⊤ U_k^(i) ||_2^2 is dimensionally consistent and matches the standard statistical definition of a (row) leverage score. Given U_k^(i) ∈ ℝ^{|D_k^(i)| × n}, the basis vector e_{i,j} must lie in ℝ^{|D_k^(i)|} (one standard basis vector per local sample), so e_{i,j}^⊤ U_k^(i) selects the j-th row of U_k^(i), which is a vector in ℝ^n; its squared Euclidean 2-norm is therefore a well-defined nonnegative scalar. This is exactly the classical leverage score h_j = ||u_j||_2^2 of the j-th sample's row in the basis/latent representation, so the notation (row selection via a basis vector) is conventional and correct. The accompanying interpretive claim (higher score ⇒ larger projection, more representative) is a qualitative statement about a definition, not a falsifiable derivable theorem, and is consistent with the standard interpretation of leverage scores. No invalid algebra, dimension mismatch, sign error, or domain violation is present: the expression is a norm squared and can never be negative. As a definition, nothing further is provable or refutable from the snippet alone.

results.content: Moreover, clients send their leverage scores to the server, which aggregates them into a global vector τ^i = concat{ τ_k^(i,j) | k = 1, ..., K; j = 1, ..., n_k^i } and normalizes it to obtain a sampling distribution:  p_k^(i,j) = τ_k^(i,j) / Σ_{j'=1}^{n_k^i} τ_k^(i,j'). (6)
results.route_rationale: Normalisation to a sampling distribution; domain check for nonnegative denominator.

math_result.reasoning: Equation (6), p_k^(i,j) = τ_k^(i,j) / Σ_{j'=1}^{n_k^i} τ_k^(i,j'), is a definitional normalization that is internally valid. Since leverage scores are squared norms, τ_k^(i,j) ≥ 0 for all j, so every p_k^(i,j) ∈ [0,1] and Σ_{j} p_k^(i,j) = 1 for each fixed (k, i). That is exactly a proper probability distribution over client k's samples for task i. There is no invalid algebra, no sign error, and no fractional manipulation error: numerator and denominator share the same index set and the sum is over the correct variable (j'), so the expression is well-typed. The only conceivable issue is that the surrounding text says the server 'aggregates them into a global vector τ^i ... and normalizes it,' whereas the printed equation normalizes within each client's block rather than over the full concatenated vector (a global normalization would need Σ_{k,j} τ_k^(i,j) in the denominator, and Σ_{k,j} p_k^(i,j) = K ≠ 1 here). However, whether the intended sampling distribution is per-client (e.g., uniform over clients, then within-client by leverage) or global cannot be determined from this snippet alone; the equation as printed is self-consistent and the per-block sums being 1 is the standard reading for sampling a client's replay data. This is a possible wording imprecision, not a provable mathematical error. The degenerate case of a zero denominator (all τ in a client equal to 0) makes the ratio undefined, but this is a trivial edge case common to every normalization definition (such samples are simply never selected) and does not invalidate the derivation; it does not rise to the level of an error requiring an erratum. Under the rule that missing surrounding context is not an error, no critical error is confirmed.

results.content: Subsequently, we perform i.i.d. sampling based on the distribution p = { p_k^(i,j) | k = 1, ..., K; j = 1, ..., n_k^i }. Once a sample x is selected, its sampling weight is adjusted to (1/√(n_s · p_x)) e_x, where n_s denotes the number of selected samples and p_x is the original sampling probability of x; e_x is the standard basis vector of x. This adjustment ensures unbiased estimation during aggregation.
results.route_rationale: Unbiased-estimation claim for the leverage-score reweighting; the one claim with real argument content, but the estimand is under-specified so a faithful Lean statement would require inventing hypotheses (faithfulness gate).

math_result.reasoning: The reweighting formula (1/√(n_s·p_x)) exactly matches the standard Drineas–Mahoney leverage-score row-sampling reweighting 1/√(s·p_i) for unbiased estimation of the Gram-type second-moment matrix. Verification: sample indices i.i.d. with probabilities p_i, collect s = n_s samples, and assign each sampled row the weight 1/√(s·p_i). The expected sampled outer-product matrix is E[Σ_{t=1..s} (1/(s·p_{X_t})) e_{X_t} e_{X_t}^T] = Σ_i s·p_i·(1/(s·p_i))·e_i e_i^T = Σ_i e_i e_i^T, i.e., the Gram matrix of the full set (identity when rows are standard basis vectors), so the weighted aggregation is unbiased. The exponent −1/2 is precisely what yields unbiasedness for the Gram/outer-product estimator (a weight 1/(s·p_x) would be needed for an unbiased estimator of the sum of the vectors, but that is not the claimed estimand). The paper's stated estimand ('aggregation') is under-specified, but under the standard interpretation of this literature — which the surrounding setup indicates — the formula is correct and the unbiasedness claim holds. The under-specification of the estimand is a presentation issue, not a provably invalid derivation, so no critical error warranting an erratum is established from the snippet alone.

results.content: Specifically, we use a lower temperature to sharpen logits for samples from earlier tasks. Furthermore, to further amplify the optimization effect of tail-class samples during training, we also leverage a re-weighted cross-entropy loss, i.e.,  L_TTS = (1/(N_old + N_new)) × ( ω_old Σ_{i=1}^{N_old} CE(y_i, Softmax(z_i^old / τ_old)) + ω_new Σ_{j=1}^{N_new} CE(y_j, Softmax(z_j^new / τ_new)) )  (7)  Here, N_old and N_new are the number of old and new task samples; y_i and y_j are their labels; z_i^old and z_j^new are logits corresponding to old and new classes; τ_old and τ_new are temperature parameters applied separately to old and new class logits; ω_old and ω_new are sample weighting coefficients. This separate normalization clarifies temperature scaling within each task's logits before loss aggregation.
results.route_rationale: Definition of the L_TTS loss; checked for internal consistency.

math_result.reasoning: The equation is a well-formed definition of a loss function, not a falsifiable theorem. Each term is internally consistent: (1) Softmax(z_i^old / τ_old) is computed over the old-class logits only, producing a valid probability distribution over old classes; since y_i is stated to be an old-class label (one-hot over old classes), CE(y_i, Softmax(...)) = -Σ_{c ∈ old} y_i,c log p_c is well-defined, non-negative, and finite for τ_old > 0. The same holds for the new-class term. (2) The overall scaling 1/(N_old + N_new) times the weighted sum of per-sample CE terms is dimensionally consistent: the raw weighted sum has units of 'loss × samples', and the prefactor converts it to a per-sample average loss; with ω_old = ω_new = 1 it reduces exactly to the standard mean cross-entropy over all N_old + N_new samples, confirming internal consistency. (3) No domain violations: each softmax output lies in [0,1] over its own class subset, each CE term is ≥ 0, and therefore L_TTS ≥ 0. The separate normalization of old vs. new logits is a deliberate design choice (task-aware temperature scaling) that the surrounding text explicitly describes; it does not produce an invalid probability expression. The weights ω_old, ω_new are free hyperparameters — their lack of a specific normalization is a modeling choice, not an algebraic error. There is no invalid algebra, no fractional/denominator mistake, no sign propagation issue, and no variable/inverse-operation error. Temperature τ > 0 is implicitly assumed (standard for softmax), and the snippet itself offers no ground to question it. Consequently, no critical mathematical error is present.

results.content: Stage 1: Initial Task Optimization. In the first task, client k learns from local data using the standard cross-entropy loss, i.e.,  min_{θ_k} (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^{N} CE(y_i, Softmax(f_{θ_k}(x_i))),  (8)
results.route_rationale: Standard cross-entropy training objective; trivial definition.

math_result.reasoning: The equation min_{θ_k} (1/N) Σ_{i=1}^{N} CE(y_i, Softmax(f_{θ_k}(x_i))) is the standard empirical cross-entropy minimization objective. The 1/N factor correctly implements the mean over the N training samples; Softmax is correctly applied to the logits f_{θ_k}(x_i) to produce a valid probability distribution over classes, and CE(y_i, ·) is well-defined for one-hot or class-index labels y_i. The minimization over θ_k is well-formed. The argument order in CE(y_i, Softmax(...)) is a notational convention (some texts write CE(pred, target)), not a mathematical error, and no algebraic manipulation, fractional computation, sign propagation, or domain constraint is violated: the objective is a non-negative sum of cross-entropy terms scaled by 1/N, which is internally consistent. As a definition of a training objective (not a falsifiable theorem), there is no derivation-invalidating mistake. The snippet lacks surrounding context (e.g., the precise definition of CE and the local dataset), but nothing in the snippet itself is provably incorrect.

results.content: Stage 2: Class-Incremental Optimization. As new tasks arrive and class imbalance emerges between previous and current tasks in client k, we employ L_TTS to mitigate the imbalance, i.e.,  min_{θ_k} (1/N_old) Σ_{i=1}^{N_old} ω_old · CE( y_i, Softmax( Concat( f_{θ_k}^old(x_i)/τ_old, f_{θ_k}^new(x_i)/τ_new ))) + (1/N_new) Σ_{j=1}^{N_new} ω_new · CE( y_j, Softmax( Concat( f_{θ_k}^old(x_j)/τ_old, f_{θ_k}^new(x_j)/τ_new )))  (9)  where x_i is the input sample, y_i is the corresponding ground-truth, f_{θ_k}^old(x) and f_{θ_k}^new(x) represent the outputs of the model corresponding to old and new classes, respectively. Softmax(·) converts the logits into a probability distribution.  [Cross-check: the paper presents this as the same loss L_TTS previously defined in Eq (7): L_TTS = (1/(N_old + N_new)) × ( ω_old Σ_{i=1}^{N_old} CE(y_i, Softmax(z_i^old / τ_old)) + ω_new Σ_{j=1}^{N_new} CE(y_j, Softmax(z_j^new / τ_new)) ).]
results.route_rationale: Definition of the L_TTS training objective; cross-checked against Eq (7) for consistency since both are displayed as L_TTS.

math_result.reasoning: Eq (9) is introduced with 'i.e.' as the loss L_TTS, but it is mathematically inequivalent to the paper's own definition of L_TTS in Eq (7). Two independent discrepancies: (1) Normalization. Eq (7) scales the entire bracket by 1/(N_old + N_new), giving per-old-sample weight ω_old/(N_old+N_new) and per-new-sample weight ω_new/(N_old+N_new) (total weight 1 with ω=1). Eq (9) instead normalizes each sum separately, giving per-old-sample weight ω_old/N_old and per-new-sample weight ω_new/N_new (total weight ω_old+ω_new = 2 with ω=1). The coefficients coincide only if ω_old/(N_old+N_new) = ω_old/N_old, i.e. N_new = 0, and ω_new/(N_old+N_new) = ω_new/N_new, i.e. N_old = 0 — impossible when both old and new samples are present (the very setting Stage 2 addresses). Hence the relative weighting of old vs new samples, and the gradient scale, differ between the two displayed forms. (2) Softmax support. In Eq (7) the CE for old samples is computed against Softmax(z^old/τ_old), a distribution over OLD logits only, with partition function Z_o = Σ_{c∈old} e^{z_c/τ_old}. In Eq (9) the same CE uses Softmax(Concat(f^old/τ_old, f^new/τ_new)), whose partition function Z_c = Z_o + Σ_{c∈new} e^{z_c/τ_new} strictly exceeds Z_o, so every old-class probability under Eq (9) is strictly smaller and the CE values differ in general (equality would require all new-class logits to carry zero mass, which never occurs in practice). The same argument applies to the new-sample terms. Therefore Eq (7) and Eq (9) define different loss functions while both are presented as 'L_TTS', making the core training objective of the method internally contradictory / under-specified: an implementer cannot determine which loss was actually optimized, and the reported results are not uniquely reproducible. This inconsistency in the method's central definition warrants a correction (erratum) or explicit clarification, so I flag it. The normalization mismatch (per-group vs global 1/(N_old+N_new) scaling) is a provable fraction-normalization error; the softmax-support mismatch is a definitional inconsistency — together they do not fit any single category perfectly, and 'Fractional/Rational error' is the closest (the per-term coefficients of the sums are treated as if 1/N_old and 1/N_new were interchangeable with 1/(N_old+N_new)).

results.content: Moreover, we have further clarified the computational complexity of the SVD step. Client-side iSVD costs O(n_k d^2) per client, while server-side SVD costs O(N d^2), where N = Σ_k n_k is the total number of pseudo-features.

math_result.reasoning: The snippet is a computational-complexity remark in an appendix, not an algebraic derivation, so it only warrants a flag if the complexity bound is provably wrong. (b) Server-side: for an N×d matrix with N ≥ d, the standard (thin) SVD costs O(N d^2) — this is the textbook result (e.g., Golub & Van Loan: SVD of an m×n matrix with m ≥ n is O(m n^2) flops). This claim is standard and correct. (a) Client-side: the claim O(n_k d^2) for the SVD (iSVD) of an n_k×d matrix with n_k ≥ d matches the standard tall-skinny SVD complexity, which is achievable without ever forming the n_k×n_k orthogonal factor P_k explicitly (e.g., via the Gram matrix X_k^T X_k at O(n_k d^2), a d×d eigendecomposition at O(d^3), and back-multiplication at O(n_k d^2)). The prompt's counter-analysis assumes the literal computation of X_k' = P_k X_k Q by forming the dense n_k×n_k matrix P_k and multiplying, which costs O(n_k^2 d + n_k d^2) — but the snippet itself does not state that the algorithm materializes P_k as a dense matrix and performs two explicit full matrix multiplications; it only states the complexity. The paper's claimed bound is the standard, defensible complexity for this operation in the tall regime (n_k ≫ d). Moreover, even under the most pessimistic literal reading, this is a brief appendix remark about asymptotic complexity, not a derivation-invalidating algebraic, calculus, sign, or domain error, and it does not touch the validity of any result in the paper — so per the flagging criteria (provably invalid algebra/calculus, fractional/rational errors, variable/inverse errors, sign failures, domain violations), and the rule against flagging claims unverifiable from the snippet alone, no critical mathematical error is established. Error not flagged.

findings.evidence: Eq (9), displayed with 'i.e.' as the loss $L_{TTS}$, is mathematically inequivalent to the paper's own definition of $L_{TTS}$ in Eq (7). Two discrepancies: **(1) Normalization** — Eq (7) scales the whole bracket by $1/(N_{old}+N_{new})$ (per-old-sample weight $\omega_{old}/(N_{old}+N_{new})$, per-new-sample weight $\omega_{new}/(N_{old}+N_{new})$), whereas Eq (9) normalizes each sum separately ($\omega_{old}/N_{old}$ and $\omega_{new}/N_{new}$). The coefficients agree only in the degenerate cases $N_{new}=0$ or $N_{old}=0$, never when both old and new samples are present. **(2) Softmax support** — Eq (7) evaluates old-sample CE against $\operatorname{Softmax}(z^{old}/\tau_{old})$, a distribution over *old logits only* (partition function $Z_o = \sum_{c\in old} e^{z_c/\tau_{old}}$), while Eq (9) uses $\operatorname{Softmax}(\operatorname{Concat}(f^{old}/\tau_{old},\, f^{new}/\tau_{new}))$ over *all* logits (partition function $Z_c = Z_o + \sum_{c\in new} e^{z_c/\tau_{new}} > Z_o$), so every old-class probability differs and the CE values differ in general. Hence the two displayed equations define different loss functions, so the method's core training objective is internally contradictory / under-specified and the reported results are not uniquely reproducible. The paper's main experimental claims are not invalidated by this, so it is classified as a minor error.

summary: Verified the mathematical content of the paper 'Class-wise Balancing Data Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning' (paper.md). The paper is a systems/method paper with no theorems, lemmas, or proofs; its mathematics consists of definitions (ISVD encryption Eq 1, concatenation Eq 2, full-SVD shape Eq 3, row selection Eq 4, leverage score Eq 5, normalization Eq 6, the TTS loss Eq 7, training objectives Eq 8–9), one claim with real argument content (the 1/√(n_s p_x) reweighting 'ensures unbiased estimation', which matches the standard Drineas–Mahoney Gram-matrix reweighting and is correct under that reading), and two appendix complexity bounds. 13 self-contained snippets were extracted and all were routed to informal verification (verify-math); the Lean queue is empty (N=0) because no snippet is both formalisable and non-trivial without inventing hypotheses, so no Lean project was created and no Lean failures occurred (no fallbacks). 12 of 13 snippets were clean. One confident finding: Eq (7) and Eq (9) are both presented as the loss L_TTS but are mathematically inequivalent — differing in normalization (1/(N_old+N_new) vs 1/N_old, 1/N_new) and in softmax support (old-class-only vs concatenated all-class logits) — leaving the method's core objective under-specified. This is classified minor because it does not invalidate the paper's experimental accuracy claims. Verdict: MINOR_ERRORS at confidence 0.8.
